title_en: Beijing Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation v. China Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation — dispute over payment for goods
keywords_en: civil; dispute over payment; second instance; High People's Court; Beijing; legal person; General Principles of Civil Law; whether the entrustment relationship is established; whether the statute of limitations has expired; affirm the original judgment; entrusted delivery; settlement of payment; interruption of statute of limitations; statute of limitations; dispute over payment with a gold and minerals import and export company
full_text_en:
Beijing Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation v. China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation — dispute over payment for goods

Plaintiff: Beijing Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation.

Legal Representative: Zuo Yong, General Manager of the company.

Agent ad litem: Gao Xiangjin, Officer of the company.

Defendant: China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation.

Legal Representative: Miao Gengshu, General Manager of the company.

Agent ad litem: Liu Kefu, Officer of the company.

The plaintiff, Beijing Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Beijing Minmetals), filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court against the defendant, China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation (hereinafter referred to as China Minmetals), over a dispute concerning payment for goods.

Plaintiff's Allegations: Our company, upon the entrustment of the defendant, shipped welded pipes to a non-party, Los Angeles Minmetals Metals Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as L.A. Minmetals), and the outstanding payment has never been settled. Later, when our company sought payment from L.A. Minmetals, we discovered that the payment had long been collected by the defendant. We request the court to order the defendant to return the outstanding payment of USD 410,255.73, compensate for interest losses of USD 311,794.35 for the period during which the funds were occupied, and bear the litigation costs of this case.

Defendant's Defense: The consignor of the welded pipes involved in this case is the Beijing Branch of China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation, which is a subordinate unit of our company and is a different entity from the plaintiff. The relationship between the Beijing Branch of China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation and our company is one of management and being managed, not a creditor-debtor relationship between legal persons. The plaintiff has no right to file a lawsuit against our company on behalf of that branch. The consignee of the welded pipes in this case is the non-party L.A. Minmetals, which has never remitted this payment to our company; therefore, the plaintiff can only assert its rights against L.A. Minmetals. Furthermore, the outstanding payment claimed by the plaintiff occurred in 1988 and has long exceeded the statute of limitations. The court should dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Facts Found by the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court:

On December 22, 1987, and May 17, 1988, the defendant, China Minmetals, and the non-party L.A. Minmetals entered into two contracts, numbered 88MSP-003 and 88MSP-004, respectively. The contracts stipulated that the seller was China Minmetals, the buyer was L.A. Minmetals, and the subject matter was the sale of 999 tons of welded pipes, with the payment condition being documents against payment in both contracts.

In September 1988, upon the entrustment of the defendant, China Minmetals, the plaintiff, Beijing Minmetals, exported 989.23 tons of welded pipes valued at USD 410,255.73 to L.A. Minmetals, in accordance with contracts 88MSP-003 (order No. 41-7845) and 88MSP-004 (order No. 41-7846) entered into between China Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals.

On August 16, 1995, the plaintiff, Beijing Minmetals, sent a letter to the non-party L.A. Minmetals, demanding payment of the above amount. In its reply, L.A. Minmetals confirmed that the said payment had been settled with the defendant, China Minmetals, and that the USD 1.56 million already paid to China Minmetals included the payment under the two contracts. On August 15, 1997, Beijing Minmetals sent a letter to China Minmetals demanding payment. China Minmetals received the letter but did not make payment.

It was further ascertained that the plaintiff, Beijing Minmetals, was originally the Beijing Branch of China National Metals & Minerals Import and Export Corporation, and was renamed to its current name on January 1, 1989. Prior to the name change, it already had legal person status and independently bore civil liability.

The above facts are confirmed by contracts, bills of lading, invoices, correspondence, and documents from the administrative authorities for industry and commerce.

Opinion of the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court:

The plaintiff, Beijing Minmetals, provided the court with relevant contracts and bills of lading concerning the subject matter of this dispute, which demonstrated the entrustment relationship between Beijing Minmetals and the defendant, China Minmetals, i.e., China Minmetals entrusted Beijing Minmetals to ship the welded pipes under the sales contract between China Minmetals and the non-party L.A. Minmetals. In fact, Beijing Minmetals had shipped the welded pipes as agreed. Article 84, Paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A debt represents a specific relationship of rights and obligations established between the parties concerned, either according to the terms of a contract or legal provisions. The party entitled to the rights is the creditor, and the party assuming the obligations is the debtor." Although China Minmetals did not issue a written confirmation of the debt to Beijing Minmetals, the correspondence between Beijing Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals and other evidence mutually corroborated the fact that China Minmetals owed payment to Beijing Minmetals, which established the existence of a creditor-debtor relationship between the two parties. Moreover, based on the sales contract relationship, this payment should have been settled between China Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals. Article 84, Paragraph 2 provides: "The creditor has the right to demand that the debtor perform its obligations as specified by the contract or as provided by law." Beijing Minmetals' claim against China Minmetals for payment is lawful and should be supported. Although China Minmetals disputed the debt, it failed to provide corresponding evidence; therefore, its defense that the debt does not exist is not supported. Beijing Minmetals only learned on August 16, 1995, that the payment had been collected by China Minmetals, and it demanded payment from China Minmetals on August 15, 1997. Article 140 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides: "The statute of limitations shall be interrupted by the filing of a lawsuit, by a party's demand for performance, or by the obligor's consent to perform. From the time of the interruption, the limitation period shall run anew." The defense of China Minmetals that the statute of limitations had expired is untenable. China Minmetals should immediately repay the debt to Beijing Minmetals and also compensate for the losses caused by delayed payment.

Accordingly, on April 5, 1999, the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment:

1. China Minmetals shall pay Beijing Minmetals USD 410,255.73 within ten days after the judgment becomes effective; if payment is delayed, the debt interest during the period of delayed performance shall be doubled based on the highest loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the same period.
2. China Minmetals shall pay Beijing Minmetals interest on the outstanding debt (calculated from August 16, 1995, until the date of full payment, based on the one-year deposit interest rate for corporate USD accounts) within ten days after the judgment becomes effective.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 39,867 shall be borne by China Minmetals.

China Minmetals, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, arguing: The appellant never agreed with the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, on entrusting shipment or purchasing the goods involved in this case; it never received the goods delivered by Beijing Minmetals, nor did it receive payment from L.A. Minmetals. The first-instance finding that there was an entrustment relationship between the appellant and Beijing Minmetals lacks factual basis and legal grounds. The first-instance court's determination that the appellant owed payment to Beijing Minmetals based solely on the so-called correspondence between Beijing Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals is without factual basis. According to Beijing Minmetals' claims and the facts found by the court, the time of delivery of goods and the time when payment should have been received by Beijing Minmetals was September 1988; therefore, the statute of limitations for its claim should have expired in September 1990. During this limitation period, Beijing Minmetals never asserted its rights; instead, it waited seven years, until August 16, 1995, to demand payment from L.A. Minmetals, which had clearly exceeded the statute of limitations. Moreover, neither L.A. Minmetals nor China Minmetals ever promised Beijing Minmetals to repay the debt, so there is no basis for an interruption of the statute of limitations and a new commencement. Beijing Minmetals filed the lawsuit with the court in 1998, which had already exceeded the statute of limitations, and it has thus lost its right to a favorable judgment as a matter of law. The first-instance court's finding that Beijing Minmetals' action was not time-barred is inconsistent with legal provisions and is erroneous. The appellant requests that the first-instance judgment be reversed in accordance with the law, and that Beijing Minmetals' claims be dismissed to protect the appellant's lawful rights and interests.

Beijing Minmetals responded: The appellee, acting in accordance with the contracts between the appellant, China Minmetals, and L.A. Minmetals, performed the delivery obligation on behalf of China Minmetals. The factory's purchase certificate and L.A. Minmetals' receipt fax sufficiently demonstrate the entrustment contract relationship between China Minmetals and the appellee. The appellee delivered the goods on behalf of China Minmetals in execution of a foreign-related contract; therefore, a four-year statute of limitations should apply. During the limitation period, the appellee repeatedly demanded payment from China Minmetals, but to no avail. The first-instance judgment protected the lawful rights and interests of the appellee and should be upheld.

Facts Found by the Beijing High People's Court:

The welded pipes involved in this case were all supplied to the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, by the Ningyuan Steel Plant of Zhangjiakou City, Hebei Province (hereinafter referred to as Ningyuan Steel Plant). According to evidence from Ningyuan Steel Plant, the goods involved in this case were all shipped to destinations such as New Orleans, Houston, and Los Angeles in the United States. After the goods were shipped, no payment was received.

Regarding the first-instance finding that "L.A. Minmetals confirmed in its reply that the said payment had been settled with the defendant, China Minmetals, and that the USD 1.56 million already paid to China Minmetals included the payment under the two contracts," upon review, the original text of L.A. Minmetals' reply to Beijing Minmetals is: "We have received your fax of August 16. Regarding the payment for the welded pipes, we reply as follows: 1. The transaction was originally concluded between Minmetals Head Office (China Minmetals) and L.A. Minmetals, and all settlement of exchange and other matters were conducted between Head Office and L.A. Minmetals. 2. The USD 1.56 million mentioned in your letter as owed by L.A. Minmetals to Head Office was all incurred before 1991. Therefore, if there is any outstanding amount, it is included therein."

During the second-instance proceedings, the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, provided an original draft of a document prepared in mid-July 1991. The draft indicated that the document was addressed to the appellant, China Minmetals, and American Metals & Minerals Co., Ltd. (L.A. Minmetals), with the subject being a request for the remittance of export payment for welded pipes. However, Beijing Minmetals did not provide proof that either entity received the document or promised repayment.

The appellee, Beijing Minmetals, also provided a civil judgment, (1998) Gao Jing Zhong Zi No. 372, from the Beijing High People's Court, to demonstrate the business practices between Beijing Minmetals and the appellant, China Minmetals. The judgment in Case No. 372 found that between 1990 and 1991, Beijing Minmetals entrusted China Minmetals to act as an agent for exporting iron nails and wire to U.S. companies, and the parties agreed that China Minmetals would receive the foreign exchange from the sales and then transfer it to Beijing Minmetals. However, after Beijing Minmetals performed its obligation to deliver the export goods as agreed, China Minmetals failed to transfer the payment received from the U.S. company to Beijing Minmetals. On June 30, 1993, China Minmetals confirmed in a fax to the U.S. company that it still owed payment to Beijing Minmetals. On July 5, 1995, China Minmetals sent a letter to Beijing Minmetals confirming that it owed RMB 207,227.65. After Beijing Minmetals sued China Minmetals in 1997, that debt was protected by the court.

Beyond this, the Beijing High People's Court confirmed the other facts found in the first instance.

Opinion of the Beijing High People's Court:

Regarding the existence of a creditor-debtor relationship: The contracts between the appellant, China Minmetals, and L.A. Minmetals for the export of welded pipes, along with the bills of lading, invoices, evidence from Ningyuan Steel Plant, and the fax from L.A. Minmetals, all provided by the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, demonstrate that Beijing Minmetals shipped 989.23 tons of welded pipes to L.A. Minmetals in accordance with those contracts, which is an objectively existing fact. The civil judgment (1998) Gao Jing Zhong Zi No. 372 from the Beijing High People's Court also proves that such transactions between the two parties occurred more than once. The evidence submitted by Beijing Minmetals is true and should be confirmed. Since China Minmetals entrusted Beijing Minmetals to ship the welded pipes under the sales contracts between China Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals, a de facto entrustment-shipment relationship was formed between Beijing Minmetals and China Minmetals. After Beijing Minmetals shipped the goods, it acquired the right to recover the payment from China Minmetals. Therefore, a creditor-debtor relationship exists between the two parties. China Minmetals' argument on appeal that there is no creditor-debtor relationship arising from the entrustment-shipment, based on the lack of a written contract between the parties, cannot be upheld.

Regarding the statute of limitations: First, since this case arises from the failure to collect payment after the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, shipped goods upon the entrustment of the appellant, China Minmetals, it is a dispute between two Chinese legal persons and does not involve foreign elements. Therefore, a four-year statute of limitations is not applicable; instead, the two-year statute of limitations provided in the General Principles of the Civil Law shall apply. Beijing Minmetals' defense that this case should be subject to a four-year statute of limitations by analogy to foreign-related contract cases lacks legal basis and cannot be upheld. Second, Beijing Minmetals performed the obligation to ship goods to L.A. Minmetals upon the entrustment of China Minmetals and in accordance with the sales contracts 88MSP-003 and 88MSP-004 entered into between China Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals. Both contracts stipulated payment by documents against payment, i.e., the seller's presentation of documents (delivery of goods) was conditional upon the buyer's payment. Beijing Minmetals should have known that from the time it delivered the welded pipes to L.A. Minmetals in September 1988, China Minmetals already had the right to settle foreign exchange. Therefore, after completing its entrusted delivery obligation, Beijing Minmetals should have promptly sought payment from China Minmetals. In other words, when Beijing Minmetals did not receive the payment transferred by China Minmetals in a timely manner after delivery, it should have known that its rights had been infringed. With respect to the debt in this case, Beijing Minmetals did not actively assert its rights within the two-year statute of limitations, as it did in Case No. (1998) Gao Jing Zhong Zi No. 372, to seek legal protection. Instead, it waited nine years until August 15, 1997, to send a letter to China Minmetals demanding payment. After receiving that letter, China Minmetals did not confirm the debt. Therefore, Beijing Minmetals' act of sending a letter demanding payment does not constitute an interruption of the statute of limitations or a new commencement. Although Beijing Minmetals submitted a draft of a demand for payment sent to China Minmetals and L.A. Minmetals in July 1991, because it failed to prove that the recipients received the letter, this evidence is not admissible. Moreover, even if the evidence were true, the two-year statute of limitations had already expired, and Beijing Minmetals cannot secure a favorable judgment. China Minmetals' argument on appeal that Beijing Minmetals' action exceeded the statutory statute of limitations is supported by facts and law and should be upheld.

The first-instance court correctly confirmed the existence of a creditor-debtor relationship arising from the entrustment-shipment between the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, and the appellant, China Minmetals. However, it erred in finding that "Beijing Minmetals learned on August 16, 1995, that the payment had been collected by China Minmetals, and demanded payment from China Minmetals on August 15, 1997, thereby interrupting the statute of limitations." Beijing Minmetals' demand for payment from China Minmetals was made long after the statute of limitations had expired, and this demand was not confirmed by China Minmetals. The first-instance judgment ordering China Minmetals to pay the outstanding debt is contrary to law and should be corrected. Beijing Minmetals was negligent in asserting its rights, and its claim against China Minmetals has exceeded the statute of limitations; as a matter of law, it has lost its right to a favorable judgment. Its claims are not supported.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 153, Paragraph 1, Items (2) and (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 153 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Beijing High People's Court rendered the following judgment on June 8, 2000:

1. The civil judgment of the first instance is reversed;
2. The claims of the appellee, Beijing Minmetals, are dismissed.

The case acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 39,867, shall be borne by the appellee, Beijing Minmetals.
